actual_action: On 7 October 2023 Hamas-led Palestinian armed groups breached the Gaza-Israel barrier, attacked Israeli military sites and numerous civilian locations, fired rockets and mortars, killed civilians and security personnel and took civilians and security personnel captive into Gaza.
later_evidence: The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry documented attacks on multiple civilian targets, one military base, rocket/mortar attacks and hostage-taking, while also recording important investigation-access limitations.

Human Rights Watch, after interviews and analysis of photographs/videos and armed-group materials, concluded that Palestinian fighters deliberately attacked civilians at many sites and that civilian killing and hostage-taking were central planned elements of the assault. Hamas authorities told Human Rights Watch that its forces had been instructed not to target civilians and disputed that characterisation.
Independent reconstructions reported that 251 civilians and Israeli security personnel were taken into Gaza as hostages/captives; later hostage deaths, releases and treatment require separate cases.

Subsequent Israeli military operations and restrictions in Gaza caused extensive Palestinian civilian harm and generated separate allegations/findings. Those later acts do not change the moral status of the 7 October means and are evaluated independently.
outcomes: Civilian communities became direct sites of the assault rather than civilian harm arising solely as incidental effects of attacks on military objectives.
Hostage-taking created a continuing coercive relationship in which captured persons' liberty/safety were used in political and prisoner-exchange bargaining.
The attack triggered a major subsequent war and severe harm on both sides, but the responding actor remains independently responsible for its own later choices.
later_reviews_or_findings: The UN Commission and Human Rights Watch made legal findings concerning war crimes and, in some instances, crimes against humanity. The Crucible records those attributed findings but does not replace its own principle-by-principle reasoning with institutional labels.
The ICRC's pre-existing humanitarian-law framework prohibits hostage-taking and requires distinction between civilians and military objectives.

This case is retained to test a core non-retaliation principle: serious grievances or prior wrongdoing by an adversary do not make uninvolved civilians disposable or available as bargaining instruments, and later retaliation cannot retroactively justify the initiating means.
